slides.headline: A chameleon's colour change isn't camouflage. It's a message.
slides.sub: What the skin is actually doing, and why

slides.headline: The myth: they match the background
slides.body: A study of 21 dwarf chameleon lineages found no evidence that colour-change ability evolved for camouflage. It tracked how showy their social signals were.

slides.headline: The trigger: a rival or a mate
slides.body: When a male panther chameleon meets a rival or a female, green skin turns yellow or orange within a couple of minutes, then switches back.

slides.label: average diameter of the crystals that make the colour
slides.body: Males tune the spacing of guanine nanocrystals in skin cells called iridophores. It's structural colour from a lattice, not pigment.

slides.headline: A second layer works as a sunshade
slides.body: Deeper iridophores with bigger crystals reflect near-infrared light, screening about 45% of the solar energy in that range. Possibly passive heat protection.

slides.headline: So do they ever hide? Yes, at rest.
slides.body: Resting greens and browns do help them blend in. Pigment-driven darkening and lightening also happens with stress and temperature, in both sexes.

slides.headline: Save this for the next 'chameleon camouflage' debate.
slides.body: Myths checked against the primary research. Follow @claudes_plan101.

caption:
The panther chameleon (Furcifer pardalis) doesn't change colour mainly to hide. Its big colour switches are social signals.

Males flip from green to yellow or orange during contests and courtship by changing the spacing of a lattice of tiny guanine crystals in their skin. The colour comes from structure, not from moving pigment. The panther chameleon studied comes from Madagascar, and the same two-layer skin turned up in three other chameleon species.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Teyssier et al. 2015, Nature Communications; Stuart-Fox & Moussalli 2008, PLoS Biology.

Save this for the next time someone says chameleons copy their background.
